name: Beth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, government or AI firms. This conversation is confidential. Beth, what is a regular workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I load fittings at the depot, check the permit and spend most of the shift replacing line parts or tracing a failed joint. I like the moment the lights come back after a careful repair. A wrong item in the stores bin can waste half the day, and it makes the low pay feel lower.

say: I would welcome a quicker **stock list** if crews still check the physical parts.
I would say the failed **line joint** still needs a person on a ladder.
think: I use **AI occasionally** for manuals, but it cannot solve our mortgage pressure.
We have **less than one month** saved for the children and household bills.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and check depot bins before departure.
Move the usual **Friday takeaway** cost into an emergency account next payday.
feel: I feel **steady at work** and pressed by household costs.
S0.quote: I do not want to learn a new screen just to save a minute and make a wrong order.
fieldNote: Beth is open to a **proven tool**, but she checks physical stock and approved manuals before trusting a screen.
Her **car battery story** makes clear that thin savings predate any major AI change.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and check parts bins before departure
Transfer the usual Friday takeaway cost into an emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster store-room list is fine as long as the bins still contain what the list says. We would still be out on the ladders replacing a failed joint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use AI to find a section in a manual, but it is no answer to our finances. Our mortgage and two school-age children leave less than a month of expenses in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my line shifts and keep checking the parts bins before leaving the depot. At the next payday I would set aside the small amount we usually spend on a Friday takeaway for emergency bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel at ease about the trade, but not about the household balance. Last winter the car battery went and we had to wait for my partner's wage to replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that emergency money cover first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use it for the car or heating before anything pleasant. We need the car to get one child to an early school club when I am on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more if the change is modest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might try the tool the stores clerk uses after she has checked it for a month. I do not want to learn a new screen just to save a minute and make a wrong order.

say: I would support **work tickets** after another crew proves they name the correct cable.
I would ask who checks **automated orders** against real poles.
think: Buying and booking staff may shrink before us, leaving **field delays** and fewer callouts.
I need **paid trial time** because the mortgage leaves little slack.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** while the first crew tests the ticket.
Join the **paid trial** after a month of correct orders and compare three tickets weekly.
feel: I feel **wary but open** to a tool that saves wasted drives.
S1.quote: A good ticket could spare a wasted drive, but an office cut dressed up as efficiency could leave our van waiting.
fieldNote: Beth waits for **one crew of evidence** before adopting a work ticket and proposes a small weekly check.
She ties **office staffing** to field delays and income, but would ask her supervisor before involving the union.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs while the first crew tests the ticket
Join the paid AI work ticket trial after a month of accurate orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that software can order parts, but somebody must compare the order with the actual pole. I would be willing to try the new work ticket once another crew has tested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying and booking staff may lose work before our line crew does. If their numbers fall, we might spend more unpaid time chasing the right fittings, and I cannot afford fewer paid callouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking repair shifts and ask to join a paid trial after the first crew reports back. In the first year I would compare three of its tickets each week with the parts we really used and bring repeated errors to the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary, not closed off. A good ticket could spare a wasted drive, but an office cut dressed up as efficiency could leave our van waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to join the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the first crew to show that the ticket names the right cable size and the safety notes are complete. If their list works for a month, I will give it a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for union help over office cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor first about how the new orders are checked. If paid field hours start falling, I would talk to the union representative about the roster.

say: I would separate **2028 work orders** from hands-on robots around 2031.
I would demand a **rainy field trial** before any crew reductions.
think: I will be **48** when robots arrive, with few nearby line jobs.
A **real vacancy** matters more than an attractive course brochure.
do: Ask about a **paid inspection course** with a funded post.
Keep paid **line shifts** after 2028 and cancel the family weekend accommodation.
feel: I feel **squeezed**, but a genuine paid vacancy gives me an option.
S2.quote: I will not spend our tiny savings learning a job the company may never offer.
fieldNote: Beth protects **paid repairs** between full thinking AI and robots, rather than treating 2028 as field job loss.
Her **conditional mobility** needs funded pay and a real post; she immediately cuts a discretionary trip for mortgage cash.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts in the first 2028 AI year
Take the company-paid inspection course if linked to a funded vacancy
Apply for the funded inspection vacancy if pay is similar
Cancel the family weekend accommodation to protect mortgage cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that full thinking AI in 2028 might write our orders, while robots able to repair lines arrive around 2031. I would ask the company to show a robot working in rain before it cuts any field shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the first date and 48 at the robot date. Three years of repairs are worth protecting, but there are few similar jobs nearby if machines eventually take the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the training office whether its paid field inspection course has an actual vacancy behind it. In the first year after 2028 I would stay on line shifts, apply for that vacancy if it is funded at similar pay, and stop booking the family weekend away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel squeezed, because the children are still in school and the mortgage does not wait. I could make a move if there were a real place to land, but not on a promise in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the weekend away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could visit my partner's parents for a day and skip the paid accommodation. I would put the unused booking money aside for the next mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection course has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the repair crew and ask what other paid roles actually exist. I will not spend our tiny savings learning a job the company may never offer.

say: I would ask for published **robot repair results** before the 2034 field change.
I would distinguish **2031 AI** in the office from robots at the lines.
think: At **51**, I may still support a child and owe on the mortgage.
A **field maintenance role** must have real site duties after AI takes report writing.
do: Request a paid **maintenance shadow day** and keep line shifts in 2031.
Apply for a **field opening** only after checking pay and duties.
feel: I feel **less rushed** and careful about unproven equipment.
S3.quote: I would not send an untested machine out alone after a storm.
fieldNote: Beth uses the longer runway to **observe work firsthand** and check whether maintenance remains physical after thinking AI.
She remains **income cautious** because household costs and a mortgage may persist at 51.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts through the first 2031 AI year
Take a paid maintenance shadow day if the depot offers one
Apply for a field maintenance vacancy after checking pay and duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to inspect a pilot properly. Full AI comes in 2031, but robots on the lines are around 2034, so I would want the company to publish its repair results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the office changes and 51 when physical robots arrive. Our older child may be leaving school by then, yet I cannot bank on no costs or an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the depot for a paid maintenance shadow day and check whether that work still needs someone in the field. In 2031 I would keep line shifts, take the shadow day if offered, and apply for an opening only after seeing its pay and duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less hurried than with the two-year warning. I could learn a new piece of equipment, but I want to see it used safely before I bet our mortgage on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a maintenance shadow day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learn more watching a fault cleared than reading a course outline. If the job is mostly reports, full AI may do it, but a field inspection would still need someone at the site until robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you support a robot trial by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with an experienced crew alongside it and a record of what fails. I would not send an untested machine out alone after a storm.

say: I would ask for **yearly field hours** before accepting claims about robot staffing.
I would separate **2036 thinking AI** from field robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume grown children or a cleared mortgage mean retirement.
A **site inspection vacancy** must involve visits, not only reports AI can write.
do: Keep paid **line work** and pay small extra mortgage principal from reliable overtime.
In **2036**, review crew hours and apply for a funded site role if shifts shrink.
feel: I feel **steadier now**, but need real figures before making retirement plans.
S4.quote: I would check whether a site-inspection opening involves actual visits or just reports AI can write.
fieldNote: Beth expects **continued paid field work** through the near term and treats the robot date as a later employment question.
She sets a **small mortgage overpayment** and a clear shift-loss trigger before considering a site inspection application.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Pay twenty-five from reliable overtime against mortgage principal
Apply for a funded site inspection opening if crew shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that ten years gives us enough time to see which machines actually stay on the job. Full thinking AI comes in 2036 and robots able to do our repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when robots arrive. The children might be working by then, but I cannot assume they will support us or that the mortgage will be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the line job and put a modest fixed amount toward mortgage principal when overtime comes. In 2036 I would review yearly field hours with my partner and apply for a funded site inspection opening if the crews had begun to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier because I expect to keep earning for several years. I would still want figures before promising my partner that we could retire when the robots show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure would make you apply?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company cut two crew shifts in a quarter and had a posted site inspection vacancy, I would look at it. I would check whether a site-inspection opening involves actual visits or just reports AI can write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would go to the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with twenty-five from each reliable overtime payment. That is small, but it will not leave the children short of school money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it leaves only about three years before robots might reach our physical work. A paid course tied to an actual field vacancy would help, along with honest trial results and enough notice to keep mortgage payments current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a course leads to work at the pole or only paperwork. I could learn a different role, but I need to know full AI has not already taken its paid tasks.

headlineQuote: I could learn a different role, but I need to know full AI has not already taken its paid tasks.
portrait: Beth is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** and adopts a tool after another crew has shown it works.
Her **thin savings** make missed callouts and routine household repairs difficult to absorb.
Across the scenarios she asks for **proven field results**, paid learning and a funded vacancy before changing roles.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves only about three years before robots could reach her physical line work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** tied to a real field vacancy and honest robot trial results would let her protect mortgage payments.
